sentences.text: Judiceratops was a large, four-legged herbivore whose name translates to "Judith River horned face".
It possessed moderately long postorbital horns that pointed forward and outward with an unusual teardrop-shaped cross-section.
The skull featured large scallops on the inner edges of its frill and a very broad, plate-like bar in the center.
Bony projections along the side edges of the frill were large near the front but became small toward the back.
This dinosaur is the oldest known member of the chasmosaurine subgroup of horned dinosaurs.
Even as the earliest representative, it already displayed distinctive group features like long, concave squamosals and pointed epioccipitals.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the basis for the species description, was recovered from the Judith River Formation in Hill County, Montana, and is now housed at the Yale Peabody Museum.
This incomplete skull includes postorbital horns, parts of the frontal, prefrontal, and lacrimal bones, the right squamosal, parietals, occipital condyle, and parts of the supraoccipital.
Researchers suggest that the rapid evolution of frill features in horned dinosaurs, including Judiceratops, was driven by sexual selection.
Taxonomically, Judiceratops is classified as a basal member of the Chasmosaurinae subfamily.
The single known species, Judiceratops tigris, lived between 78 and 77 million years ago during the middle Campanian, a period recorded as spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

It shared its environment with bony fishes, amphibians, Champsosaurus, Brachylophosaurus canadensis, Colepiocephale lambei, Dromaeosaurus, Gorgosaurus, Troodon, Albertaceratops, Medusaceratops, and Avaceratops.
No fossils of the Judiceratops lineage are known from later rocks, suggesting a pattern of rapid evolution and extinction common in late Cretaceous horned dinosaurs.
